theme: AI at Work: Start Where You Are
title: Steady in the Fog
titleHtml: Stay steady before the fog lifts.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for all Vanderbilt staff: build adaptability for seasons of change by sorting known from unknown, running small experiments while certainty catches up, and helping colleagues stay steady.
heroLead: Workplaces change faster than answers arrive, and this year AI is the loudest example. Adaptability is a skill you can practice: sort what is known from what is guessed, take one small step that buys information, and be the steady voice a colleague needs.
objectives: Sort a changing situation into known, unknown, and assumption
Design one small experiment that buys information while certainty catches up
Use grounding language that helps a worried colleague stay steady
missionTie: Defining the great university of the 21st Century means working through seasons where the answers are still forming. Staff who stay adaptable keep Exceptional Core Operations moving while the certainty catches up.
goalLead: An AI-ready workforce is mostly an adaptable one. Today builds the personal skill underneath this month's theme: moving forward on incomplete information with your footing intact.

agenda.d: The fastest way to shrink ambiguity: sort it into three honest piles.
One reversible step that buys real information this week.
What to say when a colleague is spiraling about change.

manifesto: Certainty arrives late. Adaptable people learn while they wait.

sections.headline: Ambiguity shrinks when you sort it.
sections.lead: Most change anxiety comes from treating one big fog as one big threat. Sorting breaks the fog into three piles: what is actually known, what is genuinely unknown, and what you have been assuming. The piles are always smaller than the fog.
sections.group: In pairs: name one workplace change on your mind, then each find one assumption you have been treating as a fact. 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Name one workplace change on your mind, then write one assumption you have been treating as a fact.

card.text: When change hits, write three lists: known (confirmed by someone accountable for it), unknown (nobody has decided yet), and assumed (a guess wearing a fact's clothes). Act on the first, watch the second, test the third.

interaction.q: A colleague says: 'They are bringing in AI, which means our jobs are going away.' Where does that second part belong?

opts.why: Only the first half was announced. The tool is known; the conclusion about jobs is something the fog added on the way over.

opts.t: Assumed: a guess wearing a fact's clothes
opts.why: Exactly. Fear fuses facts to conclusions. Sorting splits them apart again, and assumptions become questions you can actually ask.

opts.t: Unknown: nobody can say anything about it
opts.why: Close, but an assumption is more specific than an unknown: it is a claim someone is already acting on. Name it, then test it or ask.

sections.headline: Trade worry for a small experiment.
sections.lead: Waiting for certainty feels responsible and costs you the learning season. Adaptable people take one small, reversible step that buys information: try the tool on one chore, sit in on the new process once, ask the direct question. Small steps thin the fog.

interaction.intro: A new AI tool is rolling out in your area, and your role will change in ways nobody has fully described. Design the step you take this week.

opts.t: Wait until leadership publishes the full plan.
opts.coach: Waiting feels safe and teaches nothing. The plan will arrive eventually; your readiness can start now.

opts.t: Read everything published about the tool and the rollout.
opts.coach: Reading builds background and stays secondhand. At some point the only remaining information lives in the doing.

opts.t: Use the tool on one green-light chore from your own week.
opts.coach: One reversible, chore-sized trial. You learn what it actually does to your work, which is the exact unknown that worries people.

opts.t: Move on; you tried it and that is enough.
opts.coach: Unexamined experiments leak their value. Without one review moment, the trial becomes an anecdote rather than information.
A private note captures the learning for you alone. Sharing what you found steadies colleagues who are still waiting.

opts.t: Share one surprise and one open question with your team.
opts.coach: Now one experiment informs a whole room. Naming an open question out loud also gives colleagues permission to be mid-learning too.

heads.strong: You traded a week of worrying for a week of knowing. The unknown got smaller and your team watched it happen.
heads.mid: You learned something and kept it small. The fog thinned for you; the room around you is still guessing.
heads.weak: Another week in the fog. The plan is still coming, and your readiness stayed exactly where it was.

reactions.strong: A month later, colleagues bring their change questions to you, because you are the one who tried things. Adaptability quietly became part of your reputation.
reactions.mid: Your notes prove useful when the rollout lands, and you wish you had compared them with someone earlier. Next experiment, you close the loop out loud.
reactions.weak: The full plan finally arrives and answers half your questions. The other half were only ever answerable by trying, and that trying could have started weeks ago.

sections.headline: Be the voice that steadies.
sections.lead: In a season of change, colleagues take their cue from whoever sounds grounded. Grounding has a shape: name the known, be honest about the unknown, point at one next step. Listen to three replies to the same worry and call what each does to the room.
sections.group: In pairs: recall a change announcement that rattled your area. Which voices steadied people, and what exactly did they say? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Recall a change announcement that rattled your area. What did the steadiest voice around you actually say?

interaction.intro: A worried colleague says: 'This AI rollout is going to change everything and nobody is telling us anything.' Call what each reply does.
interaction.passMsg: You can hear the difference. Steadying names the known, admits the unknown, and offers one next step.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The tell: steadying is honest and specific. Spiraling adds heat to the guesswork; dismissing subtracts the feeling and leaves the fog.

items.q: 'Honestly, I heard it is worse than they are saying. Half the department should be worried.'
items.why: Rumor stacked on rumor. It bonds over fear for a minute and leaves everyone less steady than it found them.

items.q: 'You will be fine. Just relax; these things always blow over.'
items.why: Meant kindly, lands as dismissal. The worry goes underground, and the colleague stops bringing you real concerns.

items.q: 'Here is what is confirmed and what is still open. Want to try the tool on one small task with me this week?'
items.why: Known named, unknown admitted, one small step offered together. That is the full steadying move, and anyone can learn it.

recap.q: What is the fastest first move when a change feels overwhelming?
opts: Wait for the full official plan
Sort it into known, unknown, and assumed
Push the feeling aside and keep working
recap.why: The three piles are always smaller than the fog. Act on the known, watch the unknown, and test the assumptions.

recap.q: What makes an experiment the adaptable response to ambiguity?
opts: It is small, reversible, and buys real information
It commits the whole team at once
recap.why: The point is learning, cheaply and this week. One chore-sized trial teaches what a month of waiting never will.

recap.q: A colleague is spiraling about the AI rollout. The steadying reply...
opts: Reassures them everything will be fine
Passes along what you heard on the grapevine
Names the known, admits the unknown, offers one step
Changes the subject to lighter things
recap.why: Steadying is honest and specific. Reassurance without facts reads as dismissal, and rumors add heat to the fog.

recapMsgs.high: You have the sort, the step, and the steady voice. Point them at a real change.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Revisit the three-pile sort, then build your card.
recapMsgs.low: Worth a second pass through the three sections before you commit.

capstone.headline: Meet the fog with a move.
capstone.lead: Name the change that is actually on your mind this season. Situations and roles only, never names; nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: The change on your mind, and the assumption you most need to test.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. AI rollout in our unit; assuming my reporting work disappears

practices.name: The three-pile sort
practices.move: Write the known, unknown, and assumed lists for your change, then pick one assumption to test or ask about.

practices.name: The small experiment
practices.move: Take one reversible, chore-sized step that buys information, and share one surprise with your team.

practices.name: The steadying talk
practices.move: Find the colleague most rattled by the change. Name the known, admit the unknown, offer one small step together.

whens.out: The move happens today, while the change is loud and the learning is cheap.
The move happens this week, on your calendar by Friday.
The move becomes your standing response: the next time change news lands, you sort before you worry.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what did the step teach you that waiting would have hidden?

closing.headline: The fog is certain. So is your footing.
closing.lead: You built the sort, the small experiment, and the steadying voice. That completes this week of AI at Work: Monday's tone, Tuesday's first win, and today's skill for everything the season changes next.
closing.nextTag: Your one next step · This week
closing.nextTitle: Make the move on your card
closing.nextBody: Run it exactly as built: the sort, the step, or the steadying talk, plus one line about what it taught you. The navigator-led First-AI-Win sandbox session is a friendly place to run a small experiment with help nearby.
closing.brandline: Sort the fog. Then take the step.

facilitator.audience: All Vanderbilt staff in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; December is the AI at Work month, and this session lands even for people who missed Monday and Tuesday.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did the move on your card happen? What did it teach you that waiting would have hidden? What is your next small experiment?' Count of completed adaptability moves is the Level 3 metric for the week.

s1.title: Known, unknown, assumed
s1.purpose: Teach the three-pile sort that shrinks ambiguity into actionable pieces.
s1.say: Here is the shorthand for every change season: the fog is never as big as it feels. Most of what makes ambiguity heavy is that it arrives unsorted. So the first adaptability skill is a sorting move. Three piles: known, meaning confirmed by someone accountable for it; unknown, meaning genuinely undecided; and assumed, which is a guess wearing a fact's clothes. The piles are always smaller than the fog.
facilitate: Read the concept card aloud, once, slowly.
Run the knowledge check; ask which answer people picked before revealing.
Run the breakout: one assumption dressed up as a fact, 90 seconds each way.

ask.q: Think of a change on your own plate. What is one assumption you have been treating as a fact?
expect: Job or role fears stated as certainties
Beliefs about what leadership has decided
ask.respond: Notice how each one turns into a question the moment it is named. Assumptions are only dangerous while they stay disguised.

s1.debrief: Act on the known, watch the unknown, test the assumed. That single sort is most of what calm people are doing.
s1.watchFor: The sort turning into a gripe session about specific leaders or colleagues. Keep it on situations and roles, never names, and steer each pile toward testable statements.
s1.transition: The sort tells you where the fog is. The next skill walks into it.
s1.coreNote: Core: read the card, run the check, ask for one assumption in chat.

s2.title: The small experiment
s2.purpose: Replace waiting for certainty with one small, reversible, information-buying step.
s2.say: Here is the adaptable move nobody teaches: when you cannot get certainty, buy information. A small experiment is one reversible, chore-sized step taken this week: try the new tool on one task, sit in on the new process once, ask the direct question. This month the obvious experiment is an AI one, and Tuesday's traffic light keeps it safe: green chores, public or generic, are the perfect testing ground.
facilitate: Run Design the experiment; two minutes to make both choices and run it.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: a reversible step plus a shared close-out.

ask.q: Why does sharing one surprise with your team beat keeping the learning private?
expect: It steadies people who have yet to try
Others correct or extend what you found
ask.respond: All three. One experiment shared is a team's worth of fog cleared, which is why the close-out is half the move.

s2.debrief: Small, reversible, this week, then shared. Experiments are how adaptable people wait.
s2.watchFor: Experiments scoped too big to be safe or reversible. Shrink them out loud: if it cannot be undone or finished this week, it is a project, and projects need a plan.
s2.transition: You can steady yourself now. The last skill steadies the people around you.
s2.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

s3.title: Steady the room
s3.purpose: Give learners the steadying reply: name the known, admit the unknown, offer one step.
s3.say: Every changing workplace has two contagious moods, spiral and steady, and whichever one speaks most confidently spreads. Steadying has a learnable shape: name what is actually known, admit what is genuinely unknown, and offer one small step, ideally together. You are about to hear three replies to the same worried colleague. Call what each one does to the room.
facilitate: Run Steady or spiral? live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After the dismissive reply, pause: ask why kindness landed as shutdown.
Close with the shape typed in chat: known, unknown, one step.

ask.q: Why does 'you will be fine, just relax' fail even when it is meant kindly?
expect: It skips the person's actual question
It sounds like the speaker knows something they do not
ask.respond: Right. Comfort without content reads as dismissal. The steadying reply does more work and takes only one more sentence.

s3.debrief: Known, unknown, one step. Honest and specific beats confident and vague, every season.
s3.watchFor: The belief that steadying requires having answers. Stress the middle of the shape: admitting the unknown is what makes the known believable.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you build your own card.
s3.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the pause, take one voice on the debrief.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now make it real. One change that is actually on your mind, one assumption you need to test, one move from today. Situations and roles, never names. Build the card, pick your window, and copy it somewhere you will see it this week. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitator.closeSay: That closes the first week of AI at Work. You have Monday's tone, Tuesday's first win, and today's footing for everything the season changes next. Make your move this week and bring what it taught you back to your team. Next week Anchor's Edge rolls on with Manager Monday, and the First-AI-Win sandbox session and the LinkedIn Learning course Generative AI for Business Leaders are there all month whenever you want them. Steady the room you are in.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: The breakout surfaces a genuinely painful change, like a reorganization in progress
contingencies.then: Acknowledge it plainly and keep the tools pointed at it: the sort and the small step work hardest on real changes. Offer a follow-up conversation offline rather than processing it live.

contingencies.if: Someone challenges the premise: leadership should just communicate better
contingencies.then: Agree without surrendering the session: better communication and personal adaptability are both real needs. This hour builds the half that is in the room's control.

toughQuestions.q: Isn't this just telling us to cope with poor communication from above?
toughQuestions.a: Adaptability and good communication are complements, and this session only claims the personal half. The sort even helps you ask better questions upward: a named assumption is a question leadership can actually answer, while general anxiety is much harder to respond to.

toughQuestions.q: What if my experiment goes wrong and makes things worse?
toughQuestions.a: That is what the two design rules protect: chore-sized and reversible. On AI experiments, the traffic light adds the safety rail: green chores only, so the worst case is a draft you discard. An experiment that cannot fail safely is scoped too big; shrink it until it can.

toughQuestions.q: How do I steady a colleague when I am worried too?
toughQuestions.a: Use the shape anyway; honesty is the requirement, and calm is usually the result. Naming the known and the unknown out loud steadies the speaker as much as the listener, and offering a shared step means neither of you waits alone.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Thursday, 45 minutes on staying steady through change. Bring one workplace change that is genuinely on your mind; you will never be asked to name people. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the move happen? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did the adaptability move on your card happen? 2) What did it teach you that waiting would have hidden? 3) What is your next small experiment?
